summary: Defines a Telnet option that lets one side tell the other to turn remote flow control on or off. Flow control is how a terminal user's software starts and stops the text flowing so the screen is not overwhelmed. It was replaced by RFC 1372.

eli5.summary: When you talk to a far-away computer, sometimes the words come too fast. This is a way to say "pause" and "go ahead" so you do not get buried in words.

questions: how does telnet control flow of output
subtitle: Letting one side tell the other to pause or resume output.

tldr.problem: In Telnet sessions, output from a remote host can overwhelm the terminal, and some applications need to use all ASCII characters so traditional flow control (XOFF/XON) cannot work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1080 defines a Telnet option (code 33) that lets one side negotiate and toggle flow control on or off in the other side.
tldr.outcome: This allows hosts to control output flow from the Telnet process without consuming special characters needed by applications.

today: RFC 1080 is historic and was replaced by RFC 1372.

sections.title: The Flow Control Problem
sections.content:
Telnet is a remote terminal protocol that sends text back and forth between a client and a host. When the host sends too much output at once, the terminal can be overwhelmed. Flow control is the way to pause and resume output. Traditionally, special characters like XOFF (control-S) and XON (control-Q) signal the terminal to stop and start. However, many applications, particularly editors, need to use all possible ASCII characters as input, so reserving XOFF and XON breaks them.

The solution is to send flow control commands out of band, not as data characters. RFC 1080 defines a Telnet option to do this, allowing the host to toggle the client's flow control state without consuming any characters.
sections.eli5: Some programs need every keyboard letter for their commands. So flow control cannot use special letters. Instead, the host sends hidden commands to start and stop output.

sections.title: How the Option Works
sections.content:
The TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL option uses Telnet's standard negotiation. It has option code 33. The first phase uses WILL and DO negotiation to establish that one side (usually the host) will send flow control commands and the other side (usually the client) will obey them. Once both sides agree (after a WILL and DO exchange), the sender of the DO command can send subnegotiation commands.

As soon as negotiation completes, the side that said WILL must enable flow control. This gives a known starting state. The option can be disabled at any time by either side sending WONT or DONT.
sections.eli5: The two computers first agree that one will give orders and the other will follow. Then the first computer can send hidden start-and-stop commands.

sections.title: The Commands
sections.content:
Only two subnegotiation codes are defined: code 0 means "flow control off" and code 1 means "flow control on". Neither requires additional data. For example, the host sends the sequence IAC SB TOGGLE-FLOW-CONTROL OFF IAC SE to request that the client disable flow control, allowing all characters to pass through to the application.

The protocol is intentionally asymmetric, with the host normally sending commands and the client obeying. However, it can work in both directions if needed. Unknown subnegotiation codes must be ignored to allow future extensions.
sections.eli5: The host sends short messages like "stop sending output now" or "resume now". The client does what it is told without arguing.
